content.title: New Batch Of Student Loan Discharges Expected For 30,000 Borrowers As Final Deadline Passes
content.text: Education Secretary Linda McMahon at the White House, Tuesday, Nov. 19, 2025, in Washington. The Education Department is still fighting to delay settlement relief for student loan borrowers under the Sweet v. McMahon settlement. (AP Photo/Alex Brandon)Copyright 2025 The Associated Press. All rights reservedThe Education Department may be required to discharge the student loans for thousands of student loan borrowers after a critical deadline passed on Wednesday. If the discharges ultimately go through, it would be the final cohort of approvals for borrowers eligible for relief under the Sweet v. McMahon settlement agreement.The latest student loan discharges are expected to reach upwards of 30,000 borrowers considered to be “post-class applicants” under the settlement. And they would follow the initial batch of discharge letters sent to nearly 170,000 post-class applicants in March after the Education Department failed to convince multiple courts to extend key deadlines under the settlement agreement.But even as Wednesday’s important deadline passed, the legal battle over the Sweet v. McMahon settlement agreement continues. Here’s where things stand, and what student loan borrowers expecting relief should know.Sweet v. McMahon Settlement Requires Student Loan Discharges If Education Department Misses Key DeadlinesThe newest batch of student loan discharges, if they ultimately go through, would represent the final group of borrowers entitled to relief under the Sweet v. McMahon settlement agreement. The Education Department and a class of hundreds of thousands of borrowers entered into that agreement in 2022 to resolve longstanding allegations that the department failed to timely or fairly process applications for student loan forgiveness through Borrower Defense to Repayment. The Borrower Defense program allows borrowers to request a discharge of their student loans if their school engaged in certain kinds of fraud or other misconduct, such as misleading prospective students on a program’s competitiveness, reputation, costs, or accreditation. The Sweet v. McMahon settlement required the department to implement mass discharges for student loan borrowers who had submitted a Borrower Defense application by June 2022. A second group of borrowers, called post-class applicants, who submitted a Borrower Defense application during the five-month period after the settlement was finalized but before it was approved by the court, would be entitled to an automatic discharge of their student loans if the Education Department failed to review and adjudicate their discharge request within three years. As that three-year deadline rapidly approached, and the department appeared to be significantly behind on reviewing Borrower Defense applications, the Trump administration made last-ditch efforts to extend the Sweet v. McMahon settlement decision deadlines. But these efforts ultimately failed. Two federal district court judges rejected the Education Department’s requests for an 18-month extension. Instead, the court bifurcated post-class applicants into two groups. The initial larger group of borrowers, who must have attended one of the schools listed on an appendix included with the settlement agreement (referred to as Exhibit C), would be entitled to automatic student loan forgiveness if the department failed to adjudicate their Borrower Defense applications and issue decisions by the end of March. The department would have an additional two weeks (to April 15) to adjudicate the Borrower Defense applications for post-class applicants who had not attended an Exhibit C school. The department appealed these rulings to the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals and requested an emergency stay of the lower court’s orders, but the appeals court denied that request last month, paving the way for student loan discharges to proceed. “If you are a post-class applicant from an Exhibit C School who did not receive a decision by January 28, 2026, you are entitled to full settlement relief” and should “receive a notice from ED stating your eligibility for full settlement relief by March 30, 2026,” explained the Project on Predatory Student Lending, the legal group representing class- and post-class applicants in the Sweet v. McMahon case, on its website. “Post-class applicants who did not attend an Exhibit C school are owed a decision from ED by April 15."Tens of thousands of post-class applicants who had attended Exhibit C schools received student loan discharge notices after the Education Department missed the March 30 deadline and failed to issue them decisions on their Borrower Defense to Repayment applications.Second Sweet v. McMahon Deadline Passes, Paving The Way For More Student Loan DischargesWith the deadline for post-class applicants who did not attend Exhibit C schools now passed, covered student loan borrowers who did not receive a decision on their Borrower Defense applications by the end of the day on Wednesday should be entitled to complete settlement relief, says the Project on Predatory Student Lending. This would include student loan forgiveness, a refund of past payments made, and corrected credit reporting.“If you are a post-class applicant from a non-Exhibit C school who did not receive a decision by April 15, 2026, you are entitled to full settlement relief,” said the organization in online guidance that was updated on Thursday. Under the Sweet v. McMahon settlement agreement, the Education Department must issue discharge letters within two months, and then must discharge the student loans for covered borrowers within 12 months of that letter.“You should receive a notice from the Department confirming your eligibility for Full Settlement Relief by June 15, 2026,” said the Project on Predatory Student Lending. “Your relief should be delivered within one year of receiving that notice.”At least some post-class applicants who did not attend an Exhibit C school were indicating on public forums as of Thursday that they had not received a decision on their Borrower Defense application by the April 15 deadline.“No notice. Goodbye remaining $406k!” said one Reddit user on Thursday morning in a forum for student loan borrowers who are pursuing Borrower Defense to Repayment relief and are Sweet v. McMahon class members.“No decision via email received on 4/15,” said another. “Is it safe to kind of breathe a sigh of relief?”Legal Battle Over Student Loan Relief Under Sweet v. McMahon ContinuesBut even as all decision deadlines under the Sweet v. McMahon settlement agreement have now passed, the Education Department continues its efforts to try to delay providing student loan forgiveness and other relief to borrowers. While the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals denied the department’s request for a stay of the lower court’s rulings, the underlying appeal is still moving forward in that court.“Although the decision deadlines for the Post-Class have now passed, the Department is still trying to evade those deadlines, and it has appealed to the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals,” explained the Project on Predatory Student Lending on its website.Last week, the Education Department filed its opening brief in its appeal before the Ninth Circuit.“The Department was able to meet its January 2026 deadline only for approximately 60,000 of the 250,000 applications” considered to be post-class applicants, wrote Trump administration attorneys. “Thus, under the agreement, the Department would be required to provide more than $11 billion in automatic discharges and $600 million in refunds to the remaining applicants” if Sweet v. McMahon settlement deadlines are not extended.The district court judges that originally denied the department’s requests for an extension “improperly elevated the interests of the non-class member beneficiaries over the interests of the parties and the public in ensuring that funds are not disbursed to applicants who do not deserve them on the merits—based in substantial part on an erroneous legal conclusion that the post-class applicants were members of the class and thus parties to this case,” continued the department. “And they rested on a series of clearly erroneous factual findings and unsupported assumptions.”Student loan borrowers in the Sweet v. McMahon case have consistently argued that the Education Department voluntarily entered into the settlement agreement and has a contractual obligation to fulfill its obligations under that agreement, including by discharging the student loans for not only class members, but also for post-class applicants whose Borrower Defense applications were not reviewed by the decision deadlines. The Project on Predatory Student Lending is expected to file its response brief later this month.
